newsitem.title: UK: UK's Heseltine sees big Conservative election win.
newsitem.headline: UK's Heseltine sees big Conservative election win.

text.p: The Conservatives will win Britain's forthcoming election by at least 60 seats, deputy prime minister Michael Heseltine said on Sunday.
Heseltine, defying opinion poll forecasts that the divided and unpopular party faces a landslide defeat in the election due by May, said: "We are determined to win, we deserve to win."

Prime Minister John Major conceded on Friday that his days in office were numbered unless he can stem the tide that swept the opposition Labour Party to victory in a key by-election on Thursday, plunging the Conservatives into a minority in parliament.
But Heseltine sought to rally demoralised party workers on Sunday, telling BBC Television: "We are going to win with a majority of 60 -- nudging up."

The Conservatives, trailing Labour by at least 20 percentage points in opinion polls, hope that the "feel good factor" about Britain's buoyant economy will translate into their fifth consecutive election victory since 1979.

"We have got the fastest growing economy in western Europe. We are going to keep it that way," said Heseltine. "Unemployment in Germany went up by half a million in one month last month whereas here it has been falling for four years," he added.
Conservative morale was dealt a blow last week when Labour overturned a Conservative majority in the affluent commuter-belt constituency of Wirral South to win a by-election with a 17 percent swing.
Major, always at his best when under pressure, is now in a minority in parliament with 322 seats compared to 323 for the combined opposition.
He is expected to call the election on May 1 and to survive until then with the support of nine Ulster Unionist members of parliament from Northern Ireland.
Labour, buoyant after its by-election victory, has promised to introduce a summer budget aimed at getting the unemployed off state aid and into jobs.

Labour leader Tony Blair, who has abandoned much socialist party dogma in his bid to woo middle class voters, plans to finance new jobs with a windfall tax on the profits of recently privatised utility companies.
Conservative party chairman Brian Mawhinney said Labour's proposed early budget would bring higher taxes and bills.

"This Budget that they're talking about would be to raise tax. It would be to raise a windfall tax which means that shares would be hit, that pensions would be hit. The charges for gas, electricity, telephone, water would all go up," he said.
Chancellor of the Exchequer Kenneth Clarke accused Labour of using "Mickey Mouse Mathematics."
"This July Budget is going to raise tax and spend a lot of money on what sound like worthwhile purposes but which will damage UK Ltd by loading it with tax and costs," he added.
